content: 1. Cleaning must always precede disinfection. Items and surfaces cannot be effectively disinfected if they are not first cleaned of organic matter such as patient excretions, secretions, dirt, or soil. 2. The cleaning process should be performed in a manner that minimizes aerosolization. Cleaning alone significantly reduces the environmental bioburden. 3. Follow the manufacturer’s recommendations for the use, dilution, contact time, and handling of disinfectants. 4. Viruses and bacteria responsible for acute respiratory diseases (ARDs) can be inactivated by a variety of disinfectants. However, in some countries, regulatory agencies control the types of disinfectants available for hospital use. 5. Common hospital disinfectants include sodium hypochlorite (household bleach), alcohol, phenolic compounds, quaternary ammonium compounds, and peroxygen compounds. Sodium hypochlorite and alcohol are widely available and their use is detailed in Annex H. Cleaning the Patient-Care Environment 6. Horizontal surfaces in isolation rooms, particularly those frequently touched or near the patient’s bed, should be cleaned regularly and upon patient discharge. 7. To prevent aerosolization of ARD pathogens, damp cleaning with a moistened cloth is preferred over dry dusting or sweeping. 8. Cleaning solutions and equipment can become contaminated during wet cleaning; therefore, cleaning solutions, cloths, and mop heads should be changed frequently according to healthcare facility (HCF) policies. 9. Equipment used for cleaning and disinfection must be cleaned and dried after each use. Mop heads should be laundered daily and thoroughly dried before storage or reuse. 10. To facilitate daily cleaning, areas around the patient should be kept free of unnecessary supplies and equipment. Patient-Care Equipment 11. Reusable equipment should be disinfected and sterilized following general protocols. 12. Equipment used in isolation rooms, such as X-ray or ultrasound machines, should be disinfected with an approved hospital disinfectant before removal from the patient’s room. 13. Proper cleaning and disinfection of reusable respiratory equipment are essential in ARD patient care. Dishes and Eating Utensils 14. Reusable items should be washed in a dishwasher when possible. If dishwashers are unavailable, items should be washed by hand using detergents, with non-sterile rubber gloves worn during the process. 15. Dishes and eating utensils for the patient should be washed after each use. Disposable items should be discarded as waste, classified according to relevant state or national regulations. Linen Management 16. Heavily soiled linen should be handled with appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) to remove solid waste (e.g., feces) into a toilet before placing the linen into a laundry bag. 17. Avoid sorting linens in patient-care areas. Contaminated linen should be placed directly into a laundry bag in the isolation room with minimal manipulation to prevent contamination of air, surfaces, and persons. 18. Wash and dry linen according to routine HCF standards. For hot-water cycles, wash with detergent/disinfectant at 70°C (160°F) for at least 25 minutes. For low-temperature cycles, use a chemical suitable for proper disinfection. Waste Management 19. Waste disposal should be safe for handlers and the environment. Definitions of clinical (infectious) waste may vary by local regulations. 20. Waste should be classified and treated according to relevant state or national legislation. If waste from ARD-infected patients is classified as infectious, all waste from the patient-care area should be treated as clinical waste and disposed of per HCF policy and national regulations. 21. Liquid waste, such as urine or feces, can be flushed into the sewage system if an adequate system is in place. Packing and Transporting Contaminated Items 22. Used equipment, soiled linen, and waste should be placed directly into containers or bags in the isolation room. 23. Contain these items in a manner that prevents the containers or bags from opening or bursting during transport. Double bagging is unnecessary if the items can be placed in the bag without contaminating the outside. 24. Personnel handling these items should use Standard Precautions and perform hand hygiene after removing PPE. Prevention of Needle Stick/Sharp Injuries 25. Prevent injuries when using needles, scalpels, and other sharp instruments. Avoid recapping used needles, directing the needle point toward the body, or manually removing needles from disposable syringes. 26. Dispose of syringes, needles, and other sharp items in puncture-resistant containers located close to the area of use. Avoid using reusable syringes. Droplet Precautions 27. Respiratory pathogens transmitted via large droplets include adenovirus, human influenza, SARS, and avian influenza A (H5N1). During an influenza pandemic, droplet precautions should be applied in addition to standard precautions. 28. Use a medical mask when working within 1 meter of the patient. For practical purposes, wearing a mask when entering the patient’s room is advised. 29. Place patients in single rooms or cohort them with others with the same diagnosis. If this is not possible, maintain spatial separation of at least 1 meter. 30. Limit patient movement; patients should wear a medical mask outside their room. Airborne Precautions 31. For airborne pathogens, use a particulate respirator (e.g., N95 or equivalent) when entering the isolation room or providing care. 32. Place patients in airborne precaution rooms. If unavailable, use well-ventilated single rooms or cohort patients with the same diagnosis. 33. Aerosol-generating procedures should be performed in airborne precaution rooms with appropriate PPE. 34. Limit patient movement; patients should wear a medical mask outside their room. General Recommendations 35. Infection prevention and control measures should be tailored to the specific transmission characteristics of the pathogen and the healthcare setting.
